title: Wind Speed: mph, kph, knots, m/s, and the Beaufort Scale
h1: Wind speed conversions — mph, km/h, knots, m/s and Beaufort force
description: 1 knot = 1.852 km/h = 1.15078 mph = 0.5144 m/s. Beaufort scale runs 0–12 by v^1.5. Gusts vs sustained: WMO uses 10-min average, US uses 2-min.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

hero: A '30-knot' airport wind report is 34.5 mph or 55.6 km/h — but only if you know the reporting standard. The World Meteorological Organization averages wind over 10 minutes; the US National Weather Service averages over 2 minutes; aviation METARs use 2-minute averages but flag any gust exceeding the mean by 10 knots or more. Same wind, three different numbers.
body: Wind is measured at a standard reference height of **10 metres above open ground** (WMO 8.1.2). Every wind speed you see in a weather report, marine forecast, or aviation METAR is corrected to this height. A ground-level anemometer at 2 m reads roughly 25% lower than the 10 m equivalent — the logarithmic wind profile.
## The exact factors

> 1 knot = 1 nautical mile / hour = 1852 m / 3600 s = **0.514444 m/s exactly**
> 1 knot = **1.852 km/h exactly** (defined)
> 1 knot = 1.150779 mph
> 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h = 2.23694 mph = 1.94384 knots
> 1 mph = 1.609344 km/h = 0.868976 knots
> Round trip: 10 kt → 5.144 m/s → 18.52 km/h → 11.51 mph
## Reporting conventions — mean vs gust

| Region / use | Mean wind averaging | Gust definition | Reporting unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| WMO (global) | 10-minute mean | Peak 3-second within reporting period | m/s |
| ICAO aviation (METAR/TAF) | 2-minute mean | Peak 3-second within last 10 min, if ≥10 kt above mean | knots |
| US NWS surface obs | 2-minute mean | Peak 5-second, if ≥18 kt AND mean+9 kt above | mph or kt |
| Marine forecast (NHC/NOAA) | 1-minute mean sustained | Included in 'gusting to X' | knots (mph in bulletins) |
| Hurricane (Saffir–Simpson) | 1-minute mean at 10 m | Sustained only | mph (Atlantic) / km/h (metric) |
| Beaufort (WMO) | 10-minute mean | — | Force 0–12 |

This matters: **the same storm can be a US 'Category 4 hurricane' (155 mph 1-minute sustained) and a Chinese 'Super Typhoon' (185 km/h 10-minute sustained = 115 mph)** — the different averaging windows are the reason storms often 'lose strength' when crossing between meteorological agencies without any physical change.
## The Beaufort scale — force number to speed
Sir Francis Beaufort formalised the scale in 1805 for the Royal Navy. WMO's modern version (WMO-No. 306, 2019) is calibrated to **v = 0.836 × B^1.5 m/s** where B is Beaufort force:

| Force | m/s (10-min mean) | knots | km/h | mph | Sea/land descriptor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0–0.2 | <1 | <1 | <1 | Calm — smoke rises vertically |
| 1 | 0.3–1.5 | 1–3 | 1–5 | 1–3 | Light air — ripples |
| 2 | 1.6–3.3 | 4–6 | 6–11 | 4–7 | Light breeze — leaves rustle |
| 3 | 3.4–5.4 | 7–10 | 12–19 | 8–12 | Gentle — small flags |
| 4 | 5.5–7.9 | 11–16 | 20–28 | 13–18 | Moderate — dust, small branches |
| 5 | 8.0–10.7 | 17–21 | 29–38 | 19–24 | Fresh — small trees sway |
| 6 | 10.8–13.8 | 22–27 | 39–49 | 25–31 | Strong — large branches, umbrellas hard to use |
| 7 | 13.9–17.1 | 28–33 | 50–61 | 32–38 | Near gale — whole trees move |
| 8 | 17.2–20.7 | 34–40 | 62–74 | 39–46 | Gale — twigs break, walking difficult |
| 9 | 20.8–24.4 | 41–47 | 75–88 | 47–54 | Strong gale — chimneys, tiles fall |
| 10 | 24.5–28.4 | 48–55 | 89–102 | 55–63 | Storm — trees uprooted |
| 11 | 28.5–32.6 | 56–63 | 103–117 | 64–72 | Violent storm — widespread damage |
| 12 | ≥32.7 | ≥64 | ≥118 | ≥73 | Hurricane force |
The Saffir–Simpson hurricane scale continues past Beaufort 12: **Cat 1** 74–95 mph, **Cat 2** 96–110, **Cat 3** 111–129, **Cat 4** 130–156, **Cat 5** ≥157 mph — all US 1-minute sustained.
## The Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale — tornadoes only

## Wind pressure — force on a wall
Dynamic pressure of moving air: **q = ½ ρ v²**. At sea level ρ_air = 1.225 kg/m³:

> q (Pa) = 0.6125 × v² (m/s)  
> 10 m/s: 61 Pa
> 20 m/s (Beaufort 8): 245 Pa (5.1 lb/ft²)
> 30 m/s (Beaufort 11): 551 Pa (11.5 lb/ft²)
> 45 m/s (Category 3 hurricane): 1240 Pa (26 lb/ft²)
> 70 m/s (Category 5): 3001 Pa (63 lb/ft²)

Building codes (ASCE 7-22 in the US) specify design wind loads using a 3-second gust at 33 ft (10 m) with regional maps ranging from 90 mph inland to 180 mph on the Florida Keys. A garage door failing at 130 mph is the most common structural failure in Cat 4 hurricanes — it depressurises the house and the roof lifts.
## Wind chill
The 2001 US/Canada Wind Chill formula (Environment Canada, replaced the old 1945 Siple/Passel model):

At −10 °C (14 °F) and 30 km/h (18.6 mph), wind chill feels like −18 °C (−1 °F). Wind chill does not affect inanimate objects — a pipe won't freeze faster in the wind unless it was already warmer than ambient.
## Worked example — reading a METAR

> Wind block: 270° at 15 knots, gusting 28.
> 15 kt sustained: × 1.852 = **27.8 km/h** = × 1.1508 = **17.3 mph** = × 0.5144 = **7.72 m/s** (Beaufort 4).
> 28 kt gust: **51.9 km/h / 32.2 mph / 14.4 m/s** (Beaufort 7 as a 3-second gust).
> Aircraft crosswind component if runway is 04 (040°): sin(230°) × 15 = |sin(-130°)| × 15 = 11.5 kt crosswind — within limits for a Boeing 737 (33 kt certified).
## The five-second recap

1 kt = 1.852 km/h exactly. Beaufort force from mean wind, not gusts. WMO uses 10-min mean, US uses 2-min, hurricane scales use 1-min — never compare across systems without noting the window. Wind pressure scales as v².

faqs.q: Why do sailors and pilots use knots?
faqs.a: One knot is one nautical mile per hour, and one nautical mile equals one minute of latitude. On a chart, distance and speed line up directly — a 240-nm leg at 120 kt = 2 hours, and the latitude change matches the distance flown north/south without conversion.

faqs.q: Is 'sustained wind' the same as 'mean wind'?
faqs.a: Yes for meteorologists — 'sustained' just emphasises the averaging window. It excludes gusts and lulls.

faqs.q: What's the highest wind ever recorded on Earth?
faqs.a: Cyclone Olivia at Barrow Island, Australia (10 April 1996): 253 mph / 408 km/h / 220 knots gust. The previous record (Mount Washington 1934, 231 mph) held for 62 years.

faqs.q: Why does the same hurricane get different Cat ratings from different agencies?
faqs.a: The US uses a 1-minute mean, the WMO 10-minute mean, and Japan the 10-minute mean converted with different smoothing. A 1-min value is typically 12–14% higher than the 10-min equivalent for the same storm.

faqs.q: Do wind turbines work at Beaufort 12?
faqs.a: No — modern utility turbines have a cut-out wind speed of 25 m/s (Beaufort 9–10). Above cut-out they feather the blades and idle. The Vestas V172-7.2MW (2023) has a survival rating of 70 m/s (156 mph) with brakes locked.
